utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number, IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin, good morning to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You may sit down. Thank you. General Talic, can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I do hear you in a language that I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. And you may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I am here, Joanna Korner, assisted this morning by case manager Susan Grogan, who's sitting in for Denise Gustin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Ms. Korner. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman with Tania Radosavljevic and Marela Jevtovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. Appearances for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Natasha Ivanovic-Fauveau with Mr. Fabien Fauveau -- Mr. Fabien Masson, representing General Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There's something wrong in the air this morning. I don't know. General Talic, if at any time you're not happy with the situation of your Defence, please let me know. THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] I will let you know when I'm unhappy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, General Talic. Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I asked that Judge Draganovic just not come into court, just to sort out finally the Rule 92 for Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There's only one statement that will be tendered under Rule 92 as a result of Your Honour's rulings, which is 7.118. Your Honour ruled it was admissible subject to various redactions. I was reminded yesterday that this was, in fact, a witness for whom Your Honours granted protective measures, and so I'm really raising it at this stage to know how to deal with it. It will be exhibited, the Rule 92 statements, as I understand it. Therefore, presumably it's open, as it were, to the public. In other words, it's an exhibit in the case which could be looked at by anybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It depends on how it is exhibited.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, that's -- that's what I'm raising in a sort of rather haphazard fashion. If the -- if it is to be available to anybody who wishes to look at the records of this case, then because of the protective measures that Your Honours granted, in other words, that he would have a pseudonym and all the rest of it, we would have to equally redact - and that's why I'm raising it, so the Defence can hear it - anything that would identify him. We can certainly do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think at this particular point for sure it stands to reason. I mean -- as I see it. I don't know. Let me hear what Mr. Ackerman has to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I think as much as possible we should try to duplicate what the case would be if he in fact came here, and if the protective measures are a pseudonym, then let's substitute a pseudonym for the name that appears in the -- in the documents. The content, unless it reveals his identity, should be public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That I think we will have to go into -- I mean, because obviously I would need to go through the statement carefully, possibly the first exercise should be -- should be carried out by you, Ms. Korner. But then before it is admitted with the redactions, I would rather prefer that we go through it to make sure that there is nothing else that has been left which -- due to an oversight or whatever, which could compromise the protective measures that we have put in place.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that's what we'll do. What we'll do is, before it's exhibited, we'll do the redactions which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We think are appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see -- I mean, you can count on the cooperation of the Defence on that. I see Madam Fauveau nodding as well. So it's --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, we'll give it to Your Honours and the Defence before it's finally exhibited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so. I think that's the best way to deal with it, of dealing with it. All right?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good. Now, before we proceed -- Mr. Ackerman, I have just been given five minutes before walking into this courtroom some motions or -- one is a motion from your client, by and through you, asking this Trial Chamber to issue a redacted version of its 1st May, 2002 decision on the admission of Rule 92 bis statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That was already in my mind, and it's being taken care of. I suppose that if I find the time, after consulting my two colleagues, by the end of the day, latest tomorrow morning, we should be in the position to issue a redacted version of that decision, which does not present any major -- any major difficulties. So that the --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't see it as a -- as a matter of any urgency, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. But it's a question -- I just wanted you to know that it was already in hand, because I -- I realised that it was not a kind of decision that should remain confidential.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah. I think it's important to the jurisprudence of the Tribunal and should be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then you have a request -- a motion requesting this Trial Chamber to issue -- to issue a certificate pursuant to Rule 73 bis -- Rule 73(B), which has been amended, as you know, in order to allow for an appeal of -- against this Chamber's decision of the 6th May on Rule 70.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I haven't discussed it with my colleagues as yet because, as I said, this has just arrived this morning. Do you know anything about it or --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I haven't seen them, Your Honour, at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, it's just two paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is the statement, which obviously this Trial Chamber will need to go into, because it is at the basis of any certification that we might or might not decide upon, the statement from Mr. Ackerman or by Mr. Ackerman, that the decision of this Chamber of the 6th of May involves an issue that would significantly affect the fair and expeditious conduct of the proceedings or the outcome of the trial and that an immediate resolution by the Appeals Chamber may materially advance the proceedings. So this is something that we would await response upon from the Prosecution, and then we will -- we will discuss it and decide whether to issue a certification or not. So that is the next motion. I'm sorry I'm dealing with them but I -- have you received these already? I just was given these five minutes before the sitting. And then there is another motion for the issuance of the redaction of the Chamber's confidential decision on the alleged legality of Rule 70. Again, this is unlike the 92 bis. I had not given this matter any attention so far because, frankly, I was expecting a motion for certification in any case, so I was not bothering about this. But I will consult my two colleagues on this, and the probability is that we will come down with a redacted version of the decision on Rule 70 as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: As a pure jurisprudential matter, it's probably even more important to go into that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would think so, but I haven't discussed it with my colleagues as yet, and therefore I reserve judgement on it. So that's the position with regard to these motions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we won't trouble to respond to the two requests for redacted versions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't expect you to, Ms. Korner. It would be a waste of time. Because even for jurisprudential purposes, I mean, they should be redacted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Your Honour, it may be that the simplest way -- I haven't considered the question of a certificate for the Rule 70, but it may be the simplest way, certainly, if I agree to do it orally and even if we don't agree to do it orally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I mean, it just makes it quicker than having to go through all this again. Your Honour, on the subject of motions, can I raise one other that is still outstanding, and it affects Madam Fauveau, because this is the one where we notified the Defence that we were making an ex parte application, and Mr. Ackerman responded. When I looked at the transcript, I noticed that you invited Madam Fauveau to respond in writing, although she said that she wasn't objecting, subject -- she wanted two weeks off to do an investigation. And I don't know whether you're waiting for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. I'm not waiting for that. The only thing is this, that Mr. Ackerman, in the meantime, filed a response.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In which in subsedium he also mentioned this two weeks' break.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Should -- et cetera. So --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's why I'm anxious for a number of reasons to have a ruling. One is to discuss -- we will be saying that's unnecessary, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's being -- it's taken care of. However, with regard to Madam Fauveau, I only discovered recently - I think last Friday, I think - that -- Have you received -- because apparently due to an oversight, you were never served with a French version of the motion. And therefore, the difficulty that I had, although I took into consideration what you had stated here, was the fact that I didn't know what, or how, you were going to react to the fact that due to an oversight you had not received -- you had not been served with the French translation of the motion, which I understand was an oversight of whoever is responsible.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, quite frankly I'm not sure whether we did receive the French translation. But however, I didn't wait for the translation. And frankly speaking, I completely forgot, Your Honour, Mr. President, that I was supposed to provide a written answer. I thought that the oral answer was sufficient. If a written answer is necessary, I'll do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In fact, you did ask Madam Fauveau to respond, because it was important to put it into writing. That's on the transcript when I checked it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see. Yes, I do recall that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I do recall that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But in Your Honours don't require it, I certainly don't require it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. I don't require it. I mean, if you're happy to stick with what you had stated here -- I mean, we can proceed. I mean, this is a motion that we have been working on, and I was only marking time because I was informed at the last minute -- I mean, as you would imagine, I always check whether there are any time limits still running before I proceed, because the last thing I would want to do is to hand down a decision while one of the parties has still got a time -- legal time running. And I checked to see when you had been served with the French translation because -- and only to find out that, due to an oversight, you had not been served with the French translation. So now if you renounce to that, I think we can proceed, we can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, absolutely. I still remain with my words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. We can proceed. We will hand down the decision as soon as it is finished, actually -- yes. It should be this week, I mean, because it's already in an advanced -- in quite an advanced stage, actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Actually, it would have been handed down, had it not been for this thing that I found out. So the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Judge.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Could you -- could I kindly ask you to proceed with your solemn declaration before we go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Judge. You may sit down. Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I want this morning, please, Judge, to deal with the second transcript from the tapes that were given to you of announcement on the radio.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, that was the one that begins with the numbering 01905081. And if the B/C/S version could be handed to the witness. It starts at the top, "side A, continuation from side B, and then Vlado Vrkes. Can I just check that Your Honours have got this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, these are some further excerpts, Judge, I think it's right, from announcements that were made over the radio, particularly in respect of disarmament. And I'd like to look with you just at part of this. You will see that at the bottom of -- I don't know where it comes in the B/C/S version, but the reporter says something about "various rumours, misinformation, which sometimes raises the temperature and which has been calculated to upset the population. What do you recommend that citizens should do? Probably perhaps to listen to our radio." And this reply: "I do recommend that they listen and, and not believe the information, the rumours, the misinformation aimed at causing chaos in the Sanski Most municipality. Radio Sanski Most will broadcast daily and it is the only institution charged with conveying views and information about events in the territory of the Sanski Most municipality. I ask you to listen to Radio Sanski Most non-stop and act in accordance with the decisions broadcast on Sanski Most." Something unintelligible, "can say this is a pretty difficult and dirty war, that the Serbian people should not be a sentimental people, but fair, honest, and strong in these moments because the war that we are involved in was imposed on us, imposed from a religious standpoint, from the standpoint of a jihad. Recently you have witnessed two statements by Mr. Alija Izetbegovic calling for war of extermination. This is a religious war. This is a jihad. And the Serb people have to be strong to endure it all, have to be united to create their own state and preserve it." First, did you hear broadcast by Vlado Vrkes?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was this whilst you were in the prison or before, or both?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard it while I was in prison, but he was present in the media even before -- before the armed operation, as they called it, because Vlado Vrkes was constantly on the radio, so to speak, in these days in May, in the month of May, and also while I was in prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you hear him make statements like this, even if you didn't hear this particular broadcast, namely, that Izetbegovic was calling for a war of extermination and that it was a religious war started effectively by the Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall any such broadcast word for word, but the structure of the sentences that Vrkes used is right. This is the way he spoke at that time on the Serbian radio of Sanski Most. I listened to him on several occasions. I listened to him at the time when I still went to work, and on my way back from work in my car, on the radio, I would sometimes stop the car to listen. This is his pamphlet which was the essence of his speeches, strengthening the unity of the Serbian people, thereby encouraging people to take up arms and to start an armed conflict against Muslims and Croats, saying that we were -- what was it that he called us? -- that we wanted to have a religious war, to wage a religious war, a jihad. These are precisely the phrases that he used in his speeches, and also in the documents, in the propaganda leaflets that were plastered all over Sanski Most: In the apartments, in the public institutions, and they appeared overnight in Sanski Most. So these are the phrases, the structures, the sentences that he used. This is the kind of propaganda aimed to encourage the Serbian people to unify and to unite and to take up arms until the extermination. Because he's talking about the extermination of the Serbian people that would be perpetrated by Croats and Muslims, in order to encourage Serbs to take up arms and to start a war.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I just --

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or to go to war.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I can just interrupt for a moment from your -- before you went -- before you were imprisoned on the 25th of May, from your dealings with the Serbian population, was this propaganda effective?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was very effective, very effective, believe me. I was quite simply shocked, as a man, as a citizen of Sanski Most, as a judge, as an intellectual. In these capacities, I had many friends, real friends, and I spent more time with Serbs than with Bosniaks, in fact. This was quite accidental. I didn't make any differences -- I didn't distinguish between people. And all of a sudden in the month of May -- or rather, in April, people just turned their backs. Do you understand? It was shocking for me. It was shocking for all citizens, for all Bosniaks and Croats. People quite simply stopped contacting each other. I can remember that at my workplace in the -- in the court, the judges, of whom there were seven of Serbian nationality -- two Bosniaks had already left. They went abroad with their families.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You told us that, yes.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stayed on. They simply turned their heads away, and they would no longer come to my office. They would come to agreements of some kind among themselves. They would only establish contact among themselves, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to move, then, please, to the next page where there was an announcement - it's a male voice - that all Muslims and Croats unconditionally hand over weapons, is the beginning of the page. This in fact, as I think we'll hear later from another witness, was made by a Bosniak. But at the bottom of that page: "Armed forces. The following information has been obtained by interrogating one of the citizens. The leading extremists in the village of Capalj are..." And then it gives a number of names, Mr. Sancevic, "who is on the man and carrying a machine-gun. The following is a list of armed people in the village." It gives that list and the weapons that each of them are said to have. Now, do you know about that particular village, Capalj?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know all of these people, and I know about the village of Capalj.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: How --

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And if you'll allow me, I can say -- please go ahead and ask your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What I want to know is: These people whom you knew, did they have these weapons that were being read out on the radio?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for example, Hase Osmancevic, he was arrested on the same day that I was arrested and he was put in prison in the public security station. He was together with me in prison, and he was in Manjaca. Later, he went to Canada with his family. He was a respected businessman. He had a big industrial mill for flour. He had -- for make flour. He had a bakery, and he had a lot of employees. As far as I know, he didn't have anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It alleges --

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ramo Kazic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Pause for a moment. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It alleges that he was in possession of an anti-aircraft gun, a semi-automatic rifle, five or six zoljas, hand-held rocket launchers, an automatic rifle, three hunting rifles, a carbine, and an infrared sniper rifle, in other words, a real armory. To your knowledge from speaking to him and from what you knew of him, did he have such an armoury?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that he had none of these arms. This is pure propaganda, fabrication.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. And if we can just -- just one other name that you know about in that list. You were beginning to tell us about him.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Ramo Kazic. He's a Bosniak, between 60 and 70 years of age at that time. He was a respected businessman from the village of Capalj. And I can, with confidence, state that he didn't have any kinds of weapons. This is pure fabrication and propaganda.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And just in a sentence, what happened to that village of Capalj? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the village of Capalj fared fairly well in comparison to the other villages, because the population that left -- the people who left that village, their houses were taken over by the Serbs. Nedeljko Rasula is from that village.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, can we finally on this move to the next part, which deals with Vrhpolje. It gives what's called the list of Vrhpolje extremists. They are -- the command of the Serbian armed forces calls on the representatives to come to this meeting at the school, and so on and so forth. Then if you go - and I don't know where it's in the B/C/S - to a number of pages on, the page begins at the top of the English version: "The nearest military unit." It's page 01905087. And then we see a male voice -- I'm not sure the B/C/S -- there's a male voice, an answer beginning, "Property and people of Vrhpolje." If you just let me know when you've found it. Yes. The --

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You've found it. "The exclusive blame lies with the hodza Emir Sinanovic. I think that probably is Sinanovic, but I'm not sure that's -- I think something may have been left out. Maybe not. Is that the name -- do you know the name of the hodza, Judge?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a mistake here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The hodza's name was Emir Seferovic. He was a religious official in the village of Vrhpolje.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then it gives a list of names and goes on to say: "We are broadcasting this information on the basis of statements of the innocent inhabitants of Vrhpolje, against whom the above mentioned committed such a heinous crime that they massacred their neighbours and relatives last night. The above-mentioned individuals fled from their fellow villagers in a cowardly and underhand way, leaving them to their fate. The command of the Serbian armed forces." And again, this is repeated. It's clearly repeated over and over again. Now, Vrhpolje. From your investigations - and we're going to deal with the exhumations that we've already touched on - was there resistance in Vrhpolje by the Bosniaks and Croats?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, with regard to this male voice, I would like to say that I heard this on the Serbian radio of Sanski Most several times. On the day I was imprisoned, that was on the 27th, the 28th of May, I can remember this announcement clearly because it was broadcast several times in the course of the day and in the course of the following day. And also the policeman, the Serbian policemen, who took us out from our cells, they -- they told us about this -- or rather, that the hodza Emir Seferovic had killed two Bosniaks. These lies are terrible. This is terrible propaganda. This man didn't kill anyone. He didn't cut anyone's throat. And none of these people cut anyone's throat. These people quite simply organised themselves and they didn't want to surrender. They withdrew to a position above the village in order to defend their village, to defend their houses. They didn't want to surrender. They had infantry weapons on them. I think that all those people died. They were all killed. Because Emir Seferovic, the hodza, he was captured in a house in which he was hiding and he was imprisoned and tortured, and later on he was killed in the prison of the public station -- of the public security station in Sanski Most. And in Trnovo, he was exhumed from a mass grave. Only Ifet Hukanovic remains alive. Said Keranovic was killed. I exhumed his body. Arif Ceranic, I don't know what happened to him. Senad Huskic, he was killed. His body wasn't found. And I can't remember what happened to Mirzet Kadiric. I'll now answer the question you have asked me. As I have already said, in the village of Vrhpolje, a group of Bosniaks, just one group of Bosniaks, didn't want to surrender. They didn't want to surrender their weapons, but they defended their villages and -- their village and their houses. This village is 100 per cent Muslim, Bosniak. There are more than 500 houses in that village in over 3.000 inhabitants. These people mounted a resistance against the Serbian army. And in the forest called Galaja, these people were surrounded by the Serbian army. The units of the 6th Krajina Brigade were there and a brigade from Petrovac -- from Bosanski Petrovac was there, and the Kljuc brigade was there. And there was also a brigade from Prijedor. So Hrustovo and Vrhpolje, these villages were totally surrounded. There may have been 10.000 soldiers there with heavy artillery in the positions that they occupied. They were at full combat readiness. And at that time these people were -- at the time that this message was read over the radio, these people were completely surrounded. But what did they succeed in doing? They succeeded in -- and this was on the 2nd or the 3rd of June. They succeeded in capturing Serbian officers and soldiers, 46 of them. And this is how they saved their lives. So they were surrounded, but they captured two commanders of a battalion and their assistants and a doctor who was in the command staff of the 6th Krajina Brigade, and they then requested an exchange. And through this officer, someone called -- there was someone called Brajic, an officer in the JNA, he was a major, through him, they established contact with the command of the 6th Krajina Brigade, Colonel Branko Basara, who had a forward command post in Tramosnja, a Serbian village on the other side of the River Sana in relation to the Vrhpolje village. The commander of the 6th Krajina Brigade accepted to negotiate. This was Branko Basara. The representative of the people from the village of the Vrhpolje went to negotiations together with commander Brajic. He went to the staff of the 6th Krajina Brigade in Tramosnja, and he spent the night there with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Judge, I --

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And he managed to agree on --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. Can I -- I don't want the full account because we're going to hear evidence from people who were involved. But I just want a brief summary of those events, if you don't mind. So we don't need all the details. All I'm concerned about --

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What happened to the resistors from Vrhpolje?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This group which participated in capturing these Serbian soldiers and officers, by means of these negotiations, they managed to agree that they should be transferred to Bihac with the help of UNPROFOR. They surrendered their arms. And with UNPROFOR's help, buses were provided for them and it was made possible for them to go to Bihac. But all the others who remained in the forest and around the village and in the village, these people were all killed. There is information on this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's all I ask about this document. I think probably it ought to be exhibited together, because it's all part of the tapes. So the -- I gave an exhibit number yesterday to -- P785. So if the second transcript could be 7 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. The last one was 784.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. In that case, could it be -- the first transcript 784.1 and the second transcript we've just looked at 784.2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. And can I then go finally on the documents you produced before we deal with the exhumations -- Your Honours, these are in the big bundle. The first -- the translations begin with the number L0062786. And it's -- it's an official note signed by the judge. It's the first document. And then the second document is a list of names. The B/C/S version is 00998024 and 025.

utterances.text: It says "official note." And it's signed investigating judge Adil Draganovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It should be probably halfway through the bigger bundle. No. It's the third -- in the big bundle that had all these lists of numbers, it's the third document. utterances.text: Your Honour, I can put the English up for the moment on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can't find these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're not the only one. I have here a document which says "Record on the investigation, exhumation of bodies of Bosniaks from mass graves."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But this is not it, obviously. The only one with an "L," Ms. Korner, is --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It was disclosed to the Defence shortly before the translation -- shortly before the judge began testifying. So it was the last bunch of translations. But it's certainly in -- because your -- the registrar has produced it, so Your Honours must have it somewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It may be here, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But as I say, from now on we're only going to hand out the documents as we come to them after this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't seem to have it, Ms. Korner.

utterances.text: Can I just simply ask Your Honours to -- if you look at it on the ELMO. It's quite a short document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No image on the screen. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.text: Now, Judge, this is a document, I think, signed by you as an investigating judge; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: A list found in the Sanski Most health centre in December 1995, a list of civilians from Sanski Most who were killed in the transport of detainees to the Manjaca camp and were then sent back to Sanski Most by the same vehicle. "I hereby conclude that several individuals sent back in the same group had been alive according to statements of surviving eyewitnesses in the Manjaca camp." And, "it is hereby concluded examination was carried out by Serbian doctors." And it's a note. And then you list on the next page -- if we could just turn that over please, usher -- on the next page, the names of the various individuals. And examination is carried out by a medical committee. Very shortly, was this a list of names of people who suffocated on the way to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's a list of people who suffocated while they were being transported. They'd been taken from Betonirka in Sanski Most in a lorry. But this is not the complete number. utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Your Honours, may that then be made Prosecutor's Exhibit P785. And then he final document, and I imagine we're going to have the same problem. It's a huge document, Your Honour. It's a list of names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] P785.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And it's -- the last exhibit is P785. This one is the translation. And only a few of the actual documents have been translated, just to -- or rather, not all -- well, maybe actually all the names. I doubt it. But it's L0062909. It's in the same bundle. It's a chart of names in English, and then there's the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What is this document exactly?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's a list of people --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who were detained.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- who were detained in Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it a translation of the document that we saw yesterday that you --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- asked questions to the witness about?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. It's a different document. That was the book that was kept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And this is some kind of official list. If Your Honours -- it's being put up on the ELMO again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner. I -- I have the English version of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: With the draft translation number L0062909.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. And can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think I also have dug up the -- what seems to be a photocopy of the original.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's right. And then there are two --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which is handwritten.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. That's right. And there are two further documents enclosing further lists --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- in this bundle, a receipt which is fully translated, 03046723.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then a draft translation, I think it must be the same document. No, it's a separate document. It doesn't have a number on it, unfortunately -- but dealing with the same thing. It's headed -- one is dated -- both are dated the 23rd of August. But one has got a number 11-14-S1 and the other's 11-15-S1. And then there's a whole list of names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There are two lists of names.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. And Mr. Ackerman is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman. Sorry I didn't recognise you before.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's all right. I'm a patient man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was looking at the -- at the documents, trying to see --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- this list in both English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It was described by Ms. Korner as an official list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If I look at the B/C/S, there is absolutely nothing on that list --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I -- there is a first two lines which are illegible. I can't distinguish anything of the letters there. And perhaps -- in fact, I was going to -- I did not interrupt Ms. Korner because she was proceeding to explain some of the documents. But actually, I intended to ask her to put questions to the witness precisely on the origin of these documents, because presumably these are documents which he furnished to the Prosecution. So he should be in a position.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you have anticipated my concern, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I would object --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I mean, it's not your concern only. It's also our concern because if these are put to us as official document, we will obviously require to know what kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We're trying to -- I was trying to identify them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. That's why I didn't interrupt you. I didn't ask you -- but I still do have a little bit of a problem, Ms. Korner. The two other documents, receipts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's start with the first one, the one which has a number 11-14-S1.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 14. I think we'd better -- I don't think the witness has got that yet. Perhaps he better have the -- the whole bundle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I would like to know is which of the lists that we still have, supposedly, should accompany that receipt because I have a list which starts with 00493223.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Another list which starts 00493314.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then another list which seems to be a photocopy of an original, 00493210.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Another list which is typed but in Serbo-Croat, 00493380; another list, 00493373; and another list, 00493732. And to be frank with you, I am not in a position to make heads or tails of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think if we could give the witness all the documents, that whole bundle, and ask him to explain in turn --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- what each of these documents is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we start, Judge, please, with the first handwritten rather bad photocopied list. Can you tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Because we have a multitude of lists --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I know. But we are --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The record -- well, there's something -- we have to figure out some way so the record understands what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I was going to butt in. This is supposedly -- Ms. Korner, just for the record, am I right in assuming that you are referring to what appears on the face of it to be the photocopy of the original to which draft document -- draft translation L0062909 refers?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the number -- although it doesn't appear on the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It doesn't appear.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But if one looks at the numbering on the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is a number on the second page.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There's a number on the second page, 00493 --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Judge, can you just tell us, that document, what is it?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, since there are quite a few lists, I would like to ask you for a little bit of patience while I find my way in all these documents. All these documents are quite clear to me, because these are the documents that I submitted to the investigators.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Take your time, Judge, because this is important.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the originals of these documents exist in Sanski Most. These are the lists of the citizens of the Sanski Most municipality -- some of the citizens of that municipality of Bosniak or Muslim ethnic background, and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes -- [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your microphone, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman -- I understand what Mr. Ackerman is saying, but I'm going to get him to go through each document. But at the moment, let him give his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But let's see what Mr. Ackerman has to say. Maybe he's coming up with something new.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The problem, Your Honour, is we are making a record here which somebody is probably going to have to deal with some day. And for a witness to say, "These are the lists," we have no idea what's in front of him, we have no idea what he's talking about when he says these are the lists. Can I assume that he has every list that is in this bundle?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, I intend to deal with this document by document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, that's what I'm hoping the witness can do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And he was asked to, but then he's not doing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So please -- let's do it bit by bit, Ms. Korner. Make sure -- I want to make sure, Judge, that you have in front of you a document which is handwritten, a very bad photocopy --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- In -- at the top. It -- the -- on the second page --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He's holding it. Your Honour, he is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But my eyesight is not that good, Ms. Korner. I can't distinguish the letters from here. Make sure that on the second page, at the top right corner, there is stamped the following numbers, 00493538.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, I would like you to restrict yourself for the time being on this document only and tell us the origin of this document. Ms. Korner put it to us that this is an official document, so perhaps you should be in a position now to explain the origin of this document and why we should consider it to be a photocopy of an official document. In other words, do you have information as to who drew up this document, what was the purpose of drawing up -- for drawing up this document, where was it preserved? This kind of information is what we require from you. Details as to the individuals are not necessary for the time being. Are you happy with that, Mr. Ackerman? I think that's the way we need to proceed. Ms. Korner is smiling, so --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm just wondering why we started this exercise in the first place. But however, now I've started, I better finish.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Judge --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Please. He's in your hands, Ms. Korner. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Judge, you've heard the question. That first document, can you tell us what it is?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard the question. This document bearing the number that you just mentioned comes from the public security station in Sanski Most. This is a list of persons who were arrested of Bosniak, Muslim, and Croat ethnic background from the territory of the municipality of Sanski Most. I don't know who made this list, but its source is the criminal investigations division of the public security station of Sanski Most or the state security sector, because they carried out the investigations or, rather, the interrogation of these persons. Here you can see the name of each person, their place of birth, the ID card, the number of their ID card, and the time when they were arrested. And in the last column, next to some names, there is a note "released" or "allowed to go home." That means that after the interrogation, that person was allowed to go home. Next to some names, there is a note -- just a moment. It says "detention M." That means detention or detained in Manjaca. And next to some names, there are no notes contained in -- contained in this column, so I'm unable to say whether these persons were in fact released or whether they went to Manjaca. But some of the names, I do recognise. I remember that they were in fact in Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In fact -- can we just deal with one on the first page of our translation, number 14 --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think that is no foundation at all. I think he has no idea. He has said, for instance, that it was -- may have been -- doesn't know who prepared it. He thinks it might have been the public security section. It might have been the state security sector. He's speculating as to what the list is beyond, you know, what one might conclude from just looking at the columns in it. I think -- I think he simply doesn't know. This was just a document that was apparently found lying around somewhere. He hasn't indicated to you that he's ever established who wrote the document, when it was written --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. In fact he said that he doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. So I think referring to names on it and having him talk about names on it is inappropriate, and I ask that it not be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But if he does know, then obviously he should, not entering into much detail. What I am querying at this point in time is the incorrect translation because he -- he said that where you have "DM" means "detained in Manjaca."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's been missed off the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And in the translation, it's been completely missed off. It seems to be translated to "remanded in custody."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. If we take the first one on our list that has the "M" on the original, Karabeg Rasim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think there's something --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Judge. Can you tell us, after the name Rasim Karabeg on that first page, what's the word there?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Karabeg Rasim, it says, "detention M," or "remanded in custody M." I can tell you all about Karabeg Rasim, whether I know -- knew him or --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Don't worry. We're not on that point yet. I know you can.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it doesn't say "M." Clearly, the translator didn't realise what the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, obviously. But the witness is telling us that "M" means Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. But the translation is not wrong. It's a way of saying, "detained, remanded in custody" is what you say, in England, anyhow. So it's not a wrong translation. It's just omitted the "M," but the witness has explained that to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Judge, may I ask you what "K" means? For example, if you look at the second page, there -- in the last column, is "pristen kuci." I don't know because I can't read the handwriting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Ismet Focak, it says here, "allowed to go K." That person was brought to the Manjaca camp and he was the first person to be allowed to go home from Manjaca to Sanski Most a few days after he had been brought to the Manjaca camp. And he's right now in Sweden. Have I made myself clear?. I mean, is what I'm saying clear?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. More or less.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, in relation to the objection --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. In relation to the objection made by Mr. Ackerman, Your Honour, this is a document found in the -- the SJB or whatever -- public security station in Sanski Most. It contains a list of names which this witness can testify to his own knowledge that he knows them, and he can go through as many examples as you like --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. But is it relevant?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is relevant -- well, it's relevant to this extent. It's one of the allegations, is that the wholesale imprisonment of the non-Serb populations in various areas, in detention camps, noncombatants and the like. Some of the witnesses that Your Honours are going to be hearing about appear -- from, appear on this list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's do it this way, because we definitely -- I definitely can't allow the testimony of the judge to go on to the extent of going through this list.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- one by one. What we need to establish is whether he is in a position, having a look at this list, to tell us that he can confirm, for example, that as far as the names of individuals that according to this list were remanded -- were sent to or detained in Manjaca, whether he is in a position to confirm this, having a look at -- at the names. But I don't want details with regard to any one of them. I mean, it's not necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right, Judge. You heard --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I take it then from your ruling that you are not agreeing that this is an official list --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Permitting him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would be deciding the matter -- the question of probative value --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- at a stage when I shouldn't be deciding it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I agree with that. I agree with that. And that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I mean, for -- for the time being and until we come to the very end of this trial, any document that is presented to me, even if it has the stamp of the most -- from the most reliable source, I will still not -- not dare say, "Yes, I'm giving it probative value. Yes, I believe it to be official." I will decide that at the right moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I just want to make it clear that my objection is to the characterisation by Ms. Korner of this as an official list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't think there is no such showing -- I have no problem with the witness basically using it as an aide-memoire to basically remind him of the names of people who he knows about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: From that standpoint, I have no problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I withdraw "official." I mean, I was trying to describe it, and I knew where it came from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Obviously.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But I certainly say this is a lot more than an aide-memoire. However, this list -- or whoever compiled it, it was found on the premises of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, that he explained.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- the police station. And it contains a list of names which this witness -- it's not an aide-memoire. It's nothing of the sort. If it was an aide-memoire, it doesn't become an exhibit. But I'm asking that it be exhibited.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, you have before you no evidence whatsoever that it's accurate, that what this says happens in fact happened. You have no evidence of that it all, none, zero. There's no evidence that the person who wrote this had any knowledge of what was going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But that's a submission -- that's a submission, Mr. Ackerman. I mean, it's a statement that you are making which would ultimately be part of our deliberations. When we come to the stage of weighing the various bits and pieces of evidence that would have been brought before -- before this Trial Chamber, including this document, we are going to weigh -- we are giving -- going to give due consideration first to the allegation of the Prosecution that this is an official document, and we will have to decide whether to give it that -- grant it that characteristic -- that attribute. And secondly, considering the testimony -- the evidence of the witness, what weight to give to this document. Again, at this point in time, this debate actually becomes rather -- not exactly useless but almost. I mean, just let the witness tell us what he knows about this document, if he knows anything about it, and then we will decide later on what weight to give to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I mean, it's just -- I don't know how to express it. If you look at it, Your Honour, it doesn't -- there is no basis upon which anyone can conclude that it has any validity at all. It doesn't have any dates on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. Nothing. But this is why --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It says he was arrested at a certain time. But when? What year?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This is why -- this is why actually I -- I know, it's only the time of arrest, it says. But this is why I asked Ms. Korner to put the question to the witness to go have a quick look at this document. I suppose that he can only be useful to this Trial Chamber insofar as the persons indicated as having been detained in Manjaca are concerned, unless he is in a position to confirm also that, for example -- I don't know, but Muharem Botic, son of Sakib, from Prijedor, was at one time arrested and then released, which I would find it almost incredible and almost very difficult to -- to digest if he were to go through this whole list and tell me that he knows each and every one of them, you know, I mean ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But Your Honour, that's the problem. If this objection is going to be made -- and I must say, of all the documents that objection has been taken to, this is the last one that I expected, because we've had other documents go in with far less provenance than this one -- then I will have to go through every single name with this witness if Your Honours are going to take the view that this -- that the probative value of this document rests on the establishing that the witness knew these people and what he can say about them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. No. That's -- don't misunderstand me. Let's take it as we should. You are tendering a document in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I am. Well, I'm attempted to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Describing this document as an official document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I take that back. I take it back, Your Honour. I wish I'd never used the expression.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't suggest it's anything more than a document found in the station, in the police station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So we'll leave it about that and forget about the officiality of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's proceed from there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But probative value, that is a different matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course, it is a different matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And therefore, if this witness can say, particularly with the ones related to Manjaca, "I know that they were there because I saw them there and I knew them." He was about to tell us something about Rasim Karabeg, I think. But Your Honour, in my view, it is an unnecessary, time-wasting thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course. I don't want to do -- to go through that exercise.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I just want the witness to have a look at this document and to tell what you say he knows about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He already has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Which he has.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, the next question is this, since the question of whether there is any indication at all as to the veracity or correctness of the contents -- of the details contained in this document-- the question I am putting to the witness is a very simple one, I suppose: Have a quick look at these names without going into the details with regard to anyone in particular. Are you in a position to illuminate this ignorant Trial Chamber as to whether it should give any probative value to this document at all, from -- based on what you can tell us? Because this is -- you are the only person so far to come forward and give evidence on this document. So if you are in a position to help us, be in a position later on to decide what value to give -- you are a judge, after all. You know what I am talking about. I mean, we will -- we will need at some point in time later on to decide on this document together with others, and we will look back to your evidence -- at your evidence, and on the basis of your evidence, should be in a position to say, "This document has some value. This document has no value." So it's in your hands. But no details with regard to individuals, because otherwise we'll never finish.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I want to talk about these documents. I claim that these lists are official documents because these documents stem from the processing of the persons that are listed here, the arrested Bosniaks and Muslims. This specific document that we are discussing right now is a list of just a certain number of persons, mostly persons that I know. Because these are the people who lived in my street in Sanski Most, my neighbours, my friends. You know who your neighbours are, so I also know who these people are. I know that some of these people were with me on the truck as we went to the Manjaca camp, and these are the people listed here. This is a document from an original binder in the public security station in Sanski Most of -- made by the service that arrested these people and made these lists, and there are also notes made by the inspectors that I know who made this list and all the other lists, because I -- because I recognise their handwriting, the handwriting of those inspectors, and I know those inspectors personally because I was a participant in all this. The original binders are in Sanski Most. They are in their original state. They had been seized from the police station in Sanski Most which we called the public security station. So I'm really quite amazed to hear that somebody may call this document anything but an official document. I'm trying to help you and to explain to you what this note in the last column means because there are some names where no note is present, yet these people were taken to the Manjaca camp. I'm not going to now mention any names. That's all I had to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's just getting ridiculous at this time point. "I know these people because these are people from where I lived, my street, my neighbours." Your Honour, look at the list: Prijedor, Prijedor, Trnovo, Bosanski Krupa, Trnovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's place of birth.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You're right, it is. I guess all these people lived on his street. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, in the light of that explanation, perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can stop there for the time being and have a break, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman might like to reconsider his objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Judge, we'll give you a break and take one ourselves as well. Thirty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner. Please proceed to the next set of documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I think I'd better just finish this one off. As I understand -- I've spoken to Mr. Ackerman and I think the objection is withdrawn. No?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, it's not withdrawn. It is well stated for the record, except for the part where I didn't know what I was talking about, and that part I withdraw. But the objection stands, Your Honour. And I think we've completed your ruling on it, and we go from here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. That's how I understood it to be as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I think, Your Honour, then I have to ask, is -- I'm going ask for the admission of this document and -- as an exhibit, and I'm also going to ask if Your Honours require further information as to its authenticity, if you like, and the fact that this witness can certainly talk about other documents -- other names on this list, because you've heard his explanation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: With regard to lists of persons detained in Manjaca, Ms. Korner, there may be some persons detained there that feature in the indictment. And if the names appear here and the witness is in a position to give us information -- but from what I gather, the only thing that he can say is that -- I don't know, but Rasim Karabeg was detained in Manjaca. Correct. That's about it. But, otherwise, if you plan to prove that Rasim Karabeg was detained in Manjaca on the basis of this document, I don't see why we should proceed any further. You know, I mean ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I think then I'm only going to ask one other -- I see Madam Fauveau is on her feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm only going to say the only other question I'm going to ask about this is whether those people that were known to him, any of them were combatants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. You can ask that question. Yes. Yes. But let's see what Madam Fauveau has to say. Yes, please, Madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to say that this list is not the list of persons detained in Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. Of course not.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is the list of persons detained in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Before we move to the next list, please, Judge, of the -- the names of the people mentioned on this list as having been arrested, were any of them, to your knowledge, fighters, resisters?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you putting this question to me?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I am. Sorry, Judge. Yes.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These people didn't participate in any kind of fighting. They were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Could we move to the next list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before we do that, this list is going to be given a number, I presume?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, please. It will be Prosecutor's Exhibit 786.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, next, could we move not to the list, but there are two documents which have, each of them, a kind of official stamp on them. One is headed "Receipt," and one is headed -- well, it's to -- it's addressed to the military investigations order. What it appears to be - and you'll correct me if I'm wrong - is the letter or a copy sending the list to the military investigation organs, then a receipt showing that delivery took place on the 24th of August. You have those documents? Have they been given to the witness?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't have those documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just take my copies for the moment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I think maybe if we put the English version up on the ELMO. [Trial Chamber confers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Judge Taya is suggesting, and I agree with her, that you refer the witness to the official number at the top right corner of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the first has no stamp number. Draft translation without -- that is the 11-15-S1. There is no ERN number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is 00493317, and perhaps he can refer to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There is?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Bottom left corner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Down at the bottom. Yes. Can we just put the English version up on the ELMO, please. All right. Let's not put the English version up on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Judge, these two documents, the letter to the military and the receipt, where did they come from?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These documents came from the public security station in Sanski Most, from the same files that I have already mentioned, so the files that include these lists.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, then, Your Honour, may those be made together, because they go together, Prosecutor's Exhibit 787.1 for the document with the number 00493317, and the second document will be 787.2, which is the one 003046723.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, the list -- the remaining list, please. Can we start with the one that has the number at the top 00493380. It's not translated. Can you just tell us what the top sentence says -- first of all, the heading.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "A list of persons who were captured during the war operations in the territory of the Serbian municipality of Sanski Most."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: First of all, where did this document come from?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document also came from the public security station in Sanski Most. It came from the same files I have already mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, could I ask you to ask the witness with regard to 787.1.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And this particular document that -- this list, whether the stamp -- whether he recognises the official stamp or the copy of the official stamp.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You'd better have it back again, then, because the B/C/S version was removed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On 787.2, it's -- I mean, at least in the copy that I have, you can barely see the words in --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I just confirm. That's 004933 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think I'm going to hand both letters back and ask him to identify -- if he's able to identify the stamp.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Judge, are you able to identify the -- the stamps that one sees on those two letters, the one sending the list and the one receipting it?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can identify them. This is a stamp from the public security station in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And does that -- the stamp that appears on the document that we're now looking at, the list of people as described captured during the war operations, is that the same stamp or a different one?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the same stamp.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. You can have those -- take the letters away again.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just looking at that first page, do you recognise the names -- any of the names on that first page?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can recognise quite a few names here. There are people included here who were suffocated in the -- in the lorry from Manjaca. I can recognise their names.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Well, we can -- you needn't bother about that because we've got the list that shows that. So we can just compare the two. All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, this first page shows that, against some of the names, there are some markings. I'd like to know whether the document as found in the security -- public security records office contained those markings already or whether these markings have been made by witness or after the discovery of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Judge, you heard the question. Could you tell us, were the markings on it when it was found?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These markings were on the document when it was found. So the copy is a -- an exact copy of the original.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you know any of the people against whom these markings are made?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. For example, under number 37, Izet Mehic. He was a policeman in the public security station, a retired policeman. He was a Bosniak, and he suffocated in the -- in the transport.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Are you able --

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Kemo Talic, who was also suffocated in the lorry transporting him. He is under number 42.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. So those people are dead, obviously. All right. I won't go through the rest, then. Could we come to the next list --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could that be made Prosecutor's Exhibit 788.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, what do you mean by the next list?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: About the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Because this first list seems to consist of one page only. But what I have been given has got another -- one, two, three, four, five, six pages.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. It's all as you see from the number sequence. It appears it ought to be one document. It runs from 80 through to 86. But I'll confirm with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You need to, because -- let me explain what my concerns are. In the second page, you again have a title with "spisak," presumably meaning a list. But the next line is not like the two lines in the first page after the word "list." So that presumably means something else, presumably, if I can understand it, people who have -- persons who have been sent to Manjaca. And that finishes the page after, and there is a list of 44 persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then you have another list which starts from number 41. And we will require an explanation for that, why it starts at 41. Then the next page, you have another list without a title again, starting from number 1. At the bottom of the page, the last one is number 40, but the next page starts with number 81, finishes at 120 and continues in the subsequent page with 129, ending with 139, and then there is a handwritten note which I don't know what it means.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So perhaps these are the questions that you ought to direct to witness so we have a clear picture, because otherwise I will not understand anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The next page in that bundle, Judge, is a list of what? What's it headed?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "A list of people who have to be released from Manjaca."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Again, where does that come from?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This list comes from the public security station in Sanski Most. It comes from the same file that I have already mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
